tier_reason: The current README only states 'up to 5x faster than GNU/Clang std::vector sort' for 8-bit elements with no table or method; the only timings are first-party tables in doc/benchmarks.md at commit e678325 (Jan 2017, removed from the doc in Jan 2018): g++ 5.2.1 x86_64, Intel Core i5-3330, Makefile default -O2, code examples/bench.cpp at that commit. That would be reproducible, but the measured 2017 radix-sort code had a 4-element sorting network that indexes b[4] (out of bounds) and was later rewritten, and the 16/32/64-bit path is still incorrect at HEAD, so the numbers-on-later-fixed-code rule caps it at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Current README (no numbers): 8-bit elements by counting sort 'up to 5x faster than GNU/Clang std::vector sort (C++)'; 16/32/64-bit elements by MSD binary radix sort '2x-3x faster than GNU/Clang qsort() (C), performing similar to GNU/Clang std::vector sort (C++)'. The author's 2017 tables (doc/benchmarks.md at commit e678325, 64-bit g++ 5.2.1, i5-3330, 1M elements inserted in ascending order then sorted 10 times, insert and cleanup included): libsrt_vector_i8 0.027646 s vs cxx_vector_i8 (std::sort) 0.137919 s, about 5.0x; u8 0.026851 vs 0.150012 s, about 5.6x; i16 0.145145 vs 0.145665 s, 1.0x; u16 0.132487 vs 0.171347 s, 1.29x; i32 0.183137 vs 0.150832 s, libsrt about 0.82x (slower); u32 0.90x; i64 and u64 0.85x (slower); 32-byte generic elements via qsort 1.265519 vs 2.052374 s, 1.62x; reverse-order input gives the same pattern; 100 elements sorted 10000 times: u8 1.85x, i8 1.15x, 16/32/64-bit libsrt 0.65x-0.83x (slower). Ratios derived from page data. No qsort() timings are published, so the 2x-3x versus qsort() has no numbers.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ 5.2.1 on Ubuntu 15.10 x86_64 (64-bit build); the doc only says the bench executable is built with 'make', which at commit e678325 means Makefile.inc defaults -pipe -O2 -fomit-frame-pointer (flags inferred from the public Makefile, not stated on the page).
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i5-3330 @3GHz, 6MB L3 (sort tables exist only for the 64-bit x86_64 run; the 32-bit and Allwinner A64 runs have no sort tables).
corrections.workload: examples/bench.cpp (now test/bench.cc): push 1,000,000 elements in ascending (or reversed) order into an srt_vector or std::vector, call sv_sort or std::sort 10 times (9 of the 10 calls sort already-sorted data), cleanup; whole sequence timed. Also 100 elements sorted 10,000 times. 8-bit values wrap to a 256-value sawtooth. No random input is ever timed.
corrections.caveats: First-party only. The README claim has no numbers; the only timings are 2017 tables (doc/benchmarks.md at commit e678325) that the author removed from the doc in January 2018 and never re-ran on the current code. Those tables support the 8-bit counting-sort claim (about 5x on i8, 5.6x on u8 against libstdc++ std::sort, an O(n) counting sort against a comparison sort), but contradict 'performing similar to std::vector sort' for 32/64-bit: libsrt was 10-18% slower there, and 16/32/64-bit was 17-35% slower on 100-element vectors. The benchmark only sorts ascending or reversed input and re-sorts already-sorted data 9 times, and the time includes insertion and cleanup. Correctness bug: the 3-element and 4-element sorting networks used by the 16/32/64-bit MSD radix sort in src/saux/ssort.c are wrong at HEAD. BUILD_SORT3 leaves [1,3,2] unchanged, BUILD_SORT4 turns [3,4,1,2] into [1,3,2,4], and sv_sort on the i32 vector [1,3,2,8,9,10,11,12] returns it unsorted (hand trace). A Python port of the HEAD algorithm misplaces 114,854 of 1,000,000 random 32-bit values, while ascending, reversed and evens-then-odds inputs (the only ones the bench and stest.c use) come out sorted. This was checked on a port, not the compiled C. The 2017 code that produced the tables had a different BUILD_SORT4 that swaps b[0]/b[3] and b[1]/b[4], reading past a 4-element block. 8-bit counting sort is correct. Generic elements fall back to qsort(). Lead URL faragon.github.io/libsrt.html is API docs only (checked via the faragon/faragon.github.io repo). Filed under sorting; the project is a general C data-structure and string library.

notes: Keep with shortcomings: the 8-bit counting-sort 5x against libstdc++ std::sort is backed by the author's 2017 table (g++ 5.2.1, i5-3330), but 16/32/64-bit libsrt was slower than std::sort in that same table, and the HEAD radix sort's 3- and 4-element networks produce unsorted output on random input (found by hand trace and a Python port, not a compiled run; the bench and unit tests only use sorted, reversed or evens-then-odds input). Not a reject because the headline 8-bit path is correct and the timed runs sorted correctly. Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause, 558 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-08-02, active.
